prompt: A school district will test whether a tutoring program raises mean math scores. The researchers want to increase the POWER of the test — the probability of detecting a real improvement. Which change does that?

choices.label: Lower the significance level from $0.05$ to $0.01$.
Hope the true improvement is smaller than expected.
Switch from a one-sided to a two-sided alternative.

hint: Power is the chance of detecting an effect that is really there. Ask which change would make a real improvement easier to spot.

hints.text: Power is the chance of detecting an effect that is really there. Ask which change would make a real improvement easier to spot.
Go through the choices: more data shrinks the standard error, a smaller $\alpha$ makes rejecting harder, a smaller true effect is harder to see, and a two-sided test splits $\alpha$ across two tails.
Only increasing the sample size raises power, so the answer is choice A.

explanation: Power rises with sample size: a bigger $n$ makes $s/\sqrt{n}$ smaller, so a real improvement produces a larger test statistic.

B lowers power — a stricter $\alpha$ means fewer rejections, including correct ones. C lowers power — small effects hide in the noise. D lowers power for detecting an increase, since the rejection region in the "increase" tail shrinks.
A is the one change that helps.

alternativeExplanations.title: The three levers
steps: Power goes UP with: larger $n$, larger $\alpha$, larger true effect size.
B moves $\alpha$ the wrong way; C moves the effect the wrong way; D is effectively a smaller $\alpha$ in the direction that matters.
